sections.h2: How does a Delaware sheriff sale work?
sections.html:
A Delaware sheriff sale is a public auction of real estate run by the county sheriff to satisfy a court judgment, usually a mortgage foreclosure or unpaid taxes. The sheriff sells to the highest bidder, and the Superior Court then confirms the sale before a deed is delivered.

Delaware has three counties, and each sheriff runs sales a little differently. The sale types you will see are mortgage foreclosure sales, tax sales (also called monition sales) and, in some counties, goods and chattels sales that involve personal property.

  • Foreclosure sales: the plaintiff's attorney gives the opening bid, then bidders raise it verbally.
  • Tax or monition sales: the county or town sells a property for unpaid taxes or fees, and the owner may redeem afterward.
  • Confirmation: the court reviews the sale before the sheriff signs a deed.

For an owner facing a sale date, the practical question is how much time is left and what the options are before the auction.

sections.h2: When and where are sheriff sales held in each county?
sections.html:
Kent County holds mortgage foreclosure sales usually on the first Thursday of the month, and Sussex County holds sales on the third Tuesday of each month at 9:30 a.m. The sales are held at government buildings, not at the property.

Kent County advertises sales in the Dover Post and the Delaware State News two weeks ahead, and tax sales are held about every three months.

sections.h2: What notice must an owner receive before a Delaware sheriff sale?
sections.html:
The sheriff must advertise the sale, and the plaintiff must send notice to interested parties. Under 10 Del. C. section 4973, notice of a real estate sale must be posted at least 10 days before the sale in 10 public places in the county, including the hundred where the property lies and each adjoining hundred, and advertised for two weeks in two newspapers.

Superior Court Civil Rule 69(g) adds a separate mailing duty. At least seven days before the sale, the plaintiff or its counsel must send notice by certified mail, return receipt requested, to lienholders, tenants, record owners and other holders of recorded interests. The notice must also be posted on a common entrance or area of the building. The rule says no sheriff's sale shall be held unless proof of mailing and posting has been filed.

A July 2026 Superior Court order shows why notice matters. In New Castle County v. Coleman, the court set aside a June 9, 2026 sale of a Newark property and denied confirmation because the first mortgage holder never received actual notice that a stay had been lifted. The court noted that the sale price was roughly half of that holder's security interest.

sections.h2: What are the payment and default rules for a successful bidder?
sections.html:
The winning bidder pays a deposit on the day of sale and the balance about a month later. If the bidder fails to pay, the deposit is forfeited and the property is resold.

  • Deposit: $4,000 in Kent County, by cashier's check, certified check or money order payable to the sheriff, applied toward the 20 percent down payment.
  • Foreclosure down payment: Kent requires the rest of the 20 percent by 2:00 p.m. on sale day, with the 80 percent balance due about 30 days later on the third Monday of the following month. Sussex requires 20 percent by 3 p.m. and the balance on the third Monday of the following month.
  • Forfeiture: Kent says a buyer who misses the 2:00 p.m. payment loses the deposit and may be barred from future sales. Sussex says failure to pay the balance forfeits the sale and the non-refundable 20 percent.
  • As-is: Sussex says properties sell as-is and sight unseen, that bidders may not trespass, and that the winner is responsible for any liens.

Neither county guarantees clear title. Both tell bidders to research the Recorder of Deeds and the Prothonotary's Office first.

Delaware also taxes the sale. Under 30 Del. C. section 5404, realty transfer tax has priority out of the proceeds of a judicial sale, except where the buyer files an affidavit that the transfer to a defaulted lender is exempt.

sections.h2: When does the Superior Court confirm a Delaware sheriff sale?
sections.html:
Under Superior Court Civil Rule 69(d), the sheriff's return is due on the third Monday of the month after the sale, objections must be filed by the first Thursday after the return date, and if there is no objection the sale is confirmed automatically the following Friday.

Sussex County describes the same rhythm for its sales, saying sales are confirmed on the first Friday after the third Monday of the following month. Kent County adds that the buyer's attorney prepares the deed after confirmation and the sheriff signs it.

After confirmation, 10 Del. C. section 4976 requires the sheriff to deliver a good and sufficient deed. Section 4985 says the real estate is discharged from liens against the defendant, except prior mortgages, to the extent the sale proceeds apply. A purchaser is entitled to rent from the day of sale under section 4978.

Ownership changes only when a proper deed is recorded, as Sussex County says on its sale page. See our guide to recording a Delaware deed for the fees and affidavits.

sections.h2: Can an owner get back money left over after a sheriff sale?
sections.html:
Possibly. If a sale brings in more than the debt, the court may hold the excess. Delaware's Superior Court runs a page called Project Rightful Owner that lists former owners, sold property addresses, court-held amounts, sale dates and case numbers for New Castle, Kent and Sussex counties.

The Delaware Code, in 10 Del. C. section 4986, says proceeds that cannot be paid because the entitled persons are absent, unknown or incompetent are paid into the court that issued the process. Payment into court discharges the selling officer from liability for that money.

The Project Rightful Owner pages point claimants to petition requirements and attorney listings. If you lost a house at a sheriff sale in the past, search the list by surname.

sections.h2: What can I do before my Delaware house goes to sheriff sale?
sections.html:
You can sell the house before the sale date, and a sale before the auction lets you keep any equity. Kent County's procedures show that tax sales have a redemption period of about 90 days, with the buyer receiving the bid back plus 15 percent if the owner redeems, while foreclosure sales have no redemption period.

In Sussex County, monition property cannot be possessed until 60 days after confirmation, and for sheriff sale property the county states that occupants are not automatically evicted. A buyer at auction should plan for that.

Steps worth taking:

  • Get the exact sale date and case number from the sheriff and the Prothonotary.
  • Ask the plaintiff's attorney for a payoff figure.
  • Consider whether a sale to a buyer who closes quickly beats the auction result.
  • Check for the loss-mitigation and mediation steps listed in the official summary above, which apply to owner-occupied homes.

A cash buyer can often close faster than an auction timeline allows, but the sale must still pay off the liens of record. Cash Home Buyers cannot promise a price and will review the numbers with you.

faqs.q: What is a sheriff sale in Delaware?
faqs.a: It is a public auction of real estate conducted by the county sheriff under a court order, usually after a mortgage foreclosure or for unpaid taxes. The sale must be confirmed by the Superior Court before a deed is delivered.

faqs.q: Is there a redemption period after a Delaware foreclosure sale?
faqs.a: Kent County says foreclosure sales have no redemption period. Tax sales do: under the Delaware Code the owner has 60 days after the court approves the sale to redeem by paying the buyer the price plus 15 percent and costs.

faqs.q: How much do I need to bid at a Delaware sheriff sale?
faqs.a: Kent and Sussex counties both require a $4,000 deposit to bid. On a foreclosure the winner then pays 20 percent of the bid in total on sale day and the balance by the third Monday of the following month.

faqs.q: Do sheriff sale buyers get the keys right away?
faqs.a: No. Sussex County says occupants are not automatically evicted and that buyers may not enter before confirmation. Ownership changes when a proper deed is recorded.

faqs.q: Can a sheriff sale be stopped or postponed?
faqs.a: Sussex County says a sale can be stayed until 9:30 a.m. on sale day. Courts can also set aside a sale for irregularities, as in New Castle County v. Coleman in 2026, so owners and lenders should watch for notice of any change.

faqs.q: Can I sell my house instead of waiting for the auction?
faqs.a: Yes. You can sell before the sale date as long as the payoff of the liens of record is covered at closing. Contact the plaintiff's attorney for a payoff figure.
